B. Leaf Complexity

rag_matches.description: Shrub or tree, 1-10(-18) m, the twigs brown; stipules deciduous (but sometimes present with submature leaves). Leaves opposite or with a cuspidate apex, often puberulent and (often) entire or serrated (with the glands of the teeth). Petiole 0.2-0.4 cm, lamina 3.5-11 cm, also hirsute on the midrib on the underside. Flowers with the pedicel articulated at the base; sepals 1/4-1/3 the length of the petals, acute to rounded at the apex, indistinctly 1-3-nerved; petals whitish to pale yellow or orange, 3.5-4.2 mm, glabrous or glabrate; stamens with the connective scale extended laterally and apically (< the total length of the anther), subentire; style 1.252 mm. Fruits 1.5-1.9 cm, slightly velvety; seeds 4-8 mm, glabrous. Wet and very wet forest, 0-600+ m; Caribbean slope and near the Continental Divide, Cordilleras of Guanacaste and Talamanca, Plains of Los Guatusos, Tortuguero, and Santa Clara, Lower Talamanca, Pacific slope N Cord. of Talamanca (Cerro Nara), S Nicoya Peninsula, P.N. Carara, Puriscal region (P.N. La Cangreja), vicinity of Palmar Norte, Gulf Dulce region, Burica Peninsula. Fl. Jan., Mar.—May, Jul., Nov. SE Hond.—Pan. [The fruits with the pedicel articulated at the base and glabrous seeds] easily distinguish Rinorea squamata from its congeners in Costa Rica with opposite leaves. Due to its densely puberulent leaf blades and (often) also hirsute on the midrib on the underside, Rinorea squamata is somewhat similar to Rinorea sylvatica, but vegetatively very different due to its smaller stipules and blades with the glands of the acicular teeth (vs. broadly conical).

Dioecious shrub or tree, to 15 m tall; trunk slender or to 20 cm dbh and deeply invaginated; stems sericeous when very young, glabrate in age, with conspicuous leaf scars. Leaves somewhat clustered at apex of branchlets; stipules caducous, to 1 cm long, sericeous, leaving a conspicuous interpetiolar line of trichomes; petioles 6-14 mm long, sericeous to glabrate; blades ovate-elliptic to obovate-elliptic, abruptly short-acuminate, usually obtuse and ± decurrent onto petiole at base, 7-13(21) cm long, 3.5-8 (12) cm wide, glabrous or with sparse long trichomes on major veins below and tufts of trichomes in axils, the margins ciliate and ± revolute.

Tree, to ca 8(10) m tall; stems terete, conspicuously lenticellate, often flexuous, glabrous but with young stems tomentose. Leaves pinnate; petioles 1-6 cm long, tomentose to glabrate; petiolules ca 5 mm long; leaflets obovate, rounded to truncate or emarginate at apex, acute at base, 6-17 cm long, 3.5-7 cm wide, densely white-tomentose below, glabrate above, serrate-dentate. Panicles dense, terminal or subterminal, racemose; sepals and petals 5; sepals ovate, tomentose, greenish; petals ± obovate, white, to 2 mm long, villous, the blades fused to the scales laterally (deeply divided in middle); stamens 8, inserted on inner edge of disk; filaments villous below middle; disk fleshy, ca 0.7 mm high, tomentose; staminate flowers with the stamens exserted, 2.5-3 mm long, the ovary abortive, pubescent, lacking style; bisexual flowers with the stamens 1.5-2 mm long, only slightly exserted, the ovary ovoid, obtusely 3-angulate, with a stout style about as long as ovary, the style and ovary together ca 3 mm long; stigmas 3, recurved, densely papillate. Capsules obovate, ± rounded to bilobed, short-stipitate, ca 1.5 cm long and 1 cm wide, pale greenish-tomentose or brown-tomentose outside, woolly inside; seeds oblong, more than 1 cm long, shiny black, the lower half covered with an orange aril. Flowers in the early rainy season (June and July). The fruits mature in September and October.

Life Form: Tree 3. Brosimum Sw., nom. cons. By C.C. Berg. Trees, monoecious or dioecious. Leaves alternate and distichous; blade leathery to chartaceous, entire, pinnate-veined; stipules completely amplexicaul and connate or semi-amplexicaul and free. Inflorescences in the axils of the leaves, bisexual or unisexual, pedunculate; receptacle globose, hemispherical, turbinate or convexly discoid, initially completely covered by peltate bracts. Staminate flowers several to numerous; perianth well developed, vestigial or absent; stamens 1-4; pistillode absent. Pistillate flowers 1-several, embedded in the receptacle; ovary adnate to the perianth; stigmas 2, filiform to vine-like. Fruits forming a drupe along with the enlarged, fleshy, and often colored receptacle. Seed large, without endosperm; cotyledons thick, equal or unequal. Approx. 15 spp. Tropical America.

Dioecious tree, to 17 m tall, to 25 cm dbh; trunk with broad, horizontal leaf scars; outer bark thin, sometimes reddish; inner bark thick, granular, tan; glabrous all over or sparsely puberulent on young stems, petioles, leaf veins below, and fruit; sap thin, copious, milky. Leaves alternate; petioles to 1(1.6) cm long; stipules lanceolate, lateral, minute, subpersistent; blades mostly oblongelliptic to obovate, abruptly long-acuminate, rounded to obtuse at base, 7-15(23) cm long, 2.5-6(10) cm wide, entire or minutely serrate near apex, slightly asperous above and below. Staminate spikes pendent, 4-6.5 cm long, ca 5-6 mm wide, very densely flowered; tepals 4, broadly oval, to ca 1.7 mm long, densely and minutely pubescent; stamens 4, 2-3 mm long, strongly inflexed in bud; filament elongating, the anther springing free to fling the powdery white pollen into the air; pistillode ca 0.5 mm long. Pistillate spikes densely grayish-velutinous, usually less than 2 cm long, the flowers 4-15 per spike, sessile, ovoid, or conic; perianth minutely 4-lobed at the narrowly opened apex, 2-4.5 mm long; style branches 2, 2-5.5 mm long, long-exserted. Drupes sessile, ovoid to globular, ca 1 cm diam, densely and minutely velutinous, red becoming purple at maturity.

Shrub or tree, 2-7(-20) m, the twigs grayish brown; stipules 0.2-0.25 cm. Opposite leaves, petiole 0.2-0.9 cm; blade to [unclear reference], scattered-1% [unclear reference]. Inflorescences with peduncle 0.4-8 cm, [unclear reference], [unclear reference]. Flowers with the articulated pedicel 1/7-1/2 of the base; sepals 1/3-1/2 the [unclear reference] coacuminate at the apex, 1-5-nerved; petals [unclear reference], extended laterally and apical-pubescent on the coast (especially distally); stamens [unclear reference], sparsely puberulent [unclear reference] (> the total length of the anther), subentire; style 1.75-2 mm. Fruits [unclear reference]; seeds 6-8 mm, puberulent. Very humid forest, often near water, 0-850 m; [unclear reference] of Agulcahs Pitilla and Talamanca, San Carlos Plains and [unclear reference]. Fl. mar.-may., nov.

Shrub, 1-1.8 m tall; stems and leaves glabrate. Stipules persistent, 3-5 mm long, bifid to near base, the lobes distant, acuminate; petioles 1-1.5 cm long; blades ± elliptic, acute to acuminate, cuneate at base, 10-16 (20) cm long, 4-6 cm wide, drying light green. Racemes short, terminal, usually to 1.5 cm long at anthesis, to 3 cm long in fruit; peduncles lacking or to 1.2 cm long; inflorescence branches, pedicels, and calyces with short, ± erect, sparse trichomes, the lowermost branches subtended by a distinct, oblong-elliptic bract ca 5 mm long; bracts green, ovate, 2-7 mm long, acute, foliate, persistent, subtending groups of 2-4(7) flowers, exceeding the flowers; flowers white, sessile, ca 3.5 mm long, the tube ca 2 mm long, the lobes oblong, to ca 1.5 mm long; filaments ca 0.5 mm long, affixed above the middle of the tube; anthers ca 1 mm long; style ca 4 mm long; stigmas 0.2 mm long. Berries ± globose, 3-4 mm diam, flattened laterally and somewhat grooved, glabrous or sparsely puberulent at least when immature; seeds 2, flat, with a deep groove on the inside surface, rounded and 4- or 5-grooved on the outside surface. Croat 11132. Apparently rare; found in the younger forest south of Fairchild Point and in the forest north of Barbour Trail. Flowers mostly from June to September, principally in July, rarely also in the dry season. The fruits mature from July to October, principally in August. In Panama, Psychotria brachybotrya is most easily confused with Psychotria involucrata Sw., a superfluous name for Psychotria officinalis (Aubl.) Sw. (Steyermark, 1972). Psychotria brachybotrya differs from Psychotria officinalis by having distinct bracts beneath the lower inflorescence branches and leaves that usually dry a lighter green. Psychotria brachybotrya usually occurs in drier areas than Psychotria officinalis, which occurs principally in premontane wet forest and tropical wet forest. Psychotria brachybotrya has also been confused with Psychotria furcata DC, but is distinguished from Psychotria furcata by its larger, lighter-colored leaves and green, rather than purple, inflorescence bracts. Psychotria brachybotrya is distributed from Panama to Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, Peru, and Bolivia; Trinidad. In Panama, Psychotria brachybotrya is ecologically variable; known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Bocas del Toro, Colon, Herrera, Panama, and Darien, from tropical dry forest in Panama, and from premontane wet forest in Colon, Panama, and Darien.

Trees or shrubs; indumentum of simple trichomes; stipules present. Leaves simple, alternate, distichous, pinnate venation, margin entire, crenate or serrate. Inflorescences are spikes, racemes, or panicles, sometimes fascicled in the axil of the leaves. Flowers usually bisexual, sometimes unisexual, zygomorphic; sepals absent or (1-) 2-6, unequal; petals absent; stamens 1; annular disc present; superior ovary, carpels 2-3, locules 1, styles 1, stigmas 2-3; parietal placentation, 1-2 ovules per locule. Fruits are capsules, generally dehiscent in 3 valves; seeds 1-2, sarcotesta or "aril" colorful and rich in oil.
The family consists of 2 genera and 14 species, with a neotropical distribution; 2 genera and 3 species in CR; 2 genera and 2 species in LS.
It is characterized by its simple, alternate, distichous leaves, the margin being entire or crenate-serrate, the tertiary venation finely perpendicular to the midrib, stipules leaving a noticeable scar upon falling, and the axillary inflorescences in spikes or spike-like, very small flowers with a single stamen.
Traditionally, the family was placed in the Order Violales, alongside families such as Passifloraceae, Flacourticaceae, Violaceae, etc. It has been related to the family Flacourtiaceae, and some authors have included it as part of the same, one of the strong characters for its distinction being the presence of flowers with a single stamen and thecae separated by a connective.
Recent molecular studies propose placing it in the expanded Order Malpighiales.
No uses are known for the species of this family.

Tree, 3-8 (15) m tall, 5-35 cm dbh; wood yellow; stems weakly striate, brown or with a thin gray flaky crust, the leaf scars 3-sided, raised. Petioles 5-11 cm long, canaliculate, somewhat swollen at apex; blades ± oblong-elliptic, long-acuminate, obtuse to rounded at base, 10-30 cm long, 5-11 cm wide, glabrous, the midrib raised above. Panicles axillary and terminal, to ca 20 cm long; pedicels to 1.5 cm long; flowers ca 1.2 cm diam, conspicuous and sweetly scented; sepals 3, reflexed at anthesis, caducous; petals 6-12, white, blunt at apex; stamens numerous, unequal, exserted; anthers slightly bifid at apex; style 4-6 mm long; stigma shortly trilobate. Capsules 1-1.5 cm diam, covered with stiff bristles, dehiscing into 3 or 4 parts to expose seed; seed usually solitary, smooth, broadly ovate, ca 7 mm long, flattened on one side, gray-coated, with a shiny, bright red, lateral aril. [Croat 6097, 7753]. Locally abundant along some areas of the shore, especially on the southern side of the island; frequent in the forest. Flowers principally in the rainy season from May to October, rarely as early as April or as late as December. The fruits mature in the early dry season (January to March). Southern Mexico to northern South America. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Chiriqui, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Chiriqui and Panama, and from tropical wet forest in Colon.

Adult plants frequent in the forest; seedlings common and recognizable by the large orbicular fimbriate stipules. Flowers in the late rainy season (August to November). The fruits mature within 1 month. Costa Rica to Peru and Brazil. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone and Colon and from premontane wet forest in the Canal Zone (Pipeline Road), Veraguas, and Panama (Cerro Jefe). [Paullinia turbacensis] is a tendriled liana; stems terete, ± glabrous, bearing conspicuous brown lenticels; sap at periphery milky, not copious. Leaves trifoliolate; petioles to 14 cm long, with marginal ribs above, glabrate; leaflets broadly elliptic, acuminate or acute at apex, attenuate to rounded at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-12 cm wide (to 23 cm long and 11 cm wide as juveniles), glabrate but with axillary tufts below, subentire to remotely crenate-dentate. Thyrses small, helicoid, to 7 cm long, solitary or clustered at nodes, often on leafless stems near the ground but occurring to 5 m high; flowers white, ca 5 mm long; petals with the scales ca two-thirds as long as petals, yellow-crested, the anterior scales bilobed, their appendages pubescent, the glands white, acute, densely pubescent; staminal cluster equaling petals; filaments densely pubescent; nectar abundant, stored near the large glands; ovary glabrous; styles pubescent. Capsules elliptic to obovate, 2 cm long, red, short-pubescent, the 3 boat-shaped valves broadly spreading to expose seeds; seeds 1-3, black, shiny, less than 1 cm long, covered on the lower half by a fleshy white aril, dangling on a thin funiculus when fully displayed.

Trees, climbing shrubs, or lianas; stipules absent. Leaves compound, odd-pinnate or trifoliate, indumentum of simple trichomes, the blade sometimes with glandular dots on the underside, margin entire; petiole and petiolules pulvinated. Inflorescences in panicles, racemes, or spike-like, axillary or terminal. Flowers bisexual, white, yellowish, or pale pink; sepals 5, valvate or imbricate; petals 5, free; stamens 10, forming a short tube at the base; ovary superior, carpels 1-5, style one per carpel; ovules 2 per carpel. Fruit in follicles, often red; seeds 1 per fruit, black, the aril bright red, yellow, white, or orange.
The family consists of 16 genera and about 300–350 species, pantropical, with a distribution center in western Africa; for tropical America, 5 genera and 108 species are known; 3 genera and 9 species in CR.
It is characterized by its compound leaves, mainly trifoliate or odd-pinnate, leaflets alternate on the rachis, sometimes with dendritic trichomes, petioles clearly pulvinated, stipules absent, and the fruit follicles with a black seed with a reddish basal aril. In vegetative form, its general appearance relates it directly to the family Fabaceae, but several of the characteristics mentioned earlier allow it to be separated.
Traditionally, the family has been placed within the Order Rosales, or in close relation to the Order Sapindales, and some have suggested a link between such Orders. However, recent molecular studies suggest that its placement is in the Order Oxalidales, along with families such as: Oxalidaceae, Cunnoniaceae, Elaeocarpaceae, etc.

Life Form: Shrub, Vine 
17. Prionostemma Miers by J.A. Lombardi. Vines or shrubs, scraggly. Leaves opposite or subopposite. Inflorescences in compound, multiflowered, pedunculated, axillary dichasiums; flowers 5-merous in the perianth, rotate; sepals free; petals spreading, fringed at the margins; disk flattened, the outer margin flattened, covering and adhering to the bases of the petals; stamens 3, the anthers 2-locular, oblong, dorsifixed, dehiscing transversely; ovary 3-locular, triangular, the ovules axillary, the style elongated, stigma 1. Capsules with free lobes, each with loculicidal dehiscence through a median fissure, the valves caducous; winged seeds, the wing papery, elliptical, longer than the seed kernel. 5 spp. Tropical America and Africa, 1 sp. in tropical America.
